answers: That is short-term memory, the middle stage of the modal model proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968). Sensory memory comes first and holds everything for a fraction of a second, and long-term memory comes last and can hold a huge amount for years or even decades. Short-term memory is the small, active store, holding only five to seven items for about fifteen to twenty seconds unless you keep rehearsing them.

Maintenance rehearsal is just repeating the information silently, like saying a phone number over and over, and it keeps the information alive in short-term memory only for as long as you keep repeating. Elaborative rehearsal links the new information to things you already know in long-term memory, like connecting a fact to an example or a personal experience. Those connections give it meaning and create several paths back to it, so it transfers into long-term memory much better.

Rehearsal is a control process because it is something the person chooses to do with the contents of memory, rather than something the memory system does automatically. You decide whether to repeat a number, how much, and for how long, and that choice changes how much you keep. Repeating information keeps it active in short-term memory and also helps move it into long-term memory. Chunking and attention strategies are other examples of control processes.

Attention is the gateway between the two stores. Sensory memory briefly takes in everything that reaches the senses, like a whole screen full of phone listings, but it fades almost at once. Attention picks out the one thing you need, like the single number, and only what attention selects passes into short-term memory. Because short-term memory is so small, this selection matters, and anything attention ignores is simply lost.

That is a memory palace, an ancient strategy that works as a control process. You picture a familiar place, like a building with many rooms, and put each item to remember at a spot along a route through it. Those places are already stored in long-term memory, so they act as ready-made cues. Then you just walk through the building in your mind, and the items come back in order.

Sperling (1960) found that whole report gave much less than partial report. In whole report, people named about 4.5 of the 12 letters, which is 37.5 percent. In partial report, where a tone told them which row to give, they named about 3.3 of the 4 letters in the cued row, or 82 percent, and they could do it for any row. So most of the letters were available at first, but the report was too slow to get them out.

What Sperling (1960) manipulated was the report method, meaning what participants had to report and when they found out. In whole report they named as many letters as they could. In partial report a tone came after the display and told them which row to report, high for the top row, medium for the middle, low for the bottom. In delayed partial report, there was a short delay before that tone. The display was three rows of four letters.

In delayed partial report the tone comes only after a short wait, and by then the icon has already faded. All the letters were registered when the display flashed, but visual sensory memory decays very fast, so only about one of the four letters in the cued row was left, around 25 percent. By about a second, the advantage of partial report was nearly gone, down to the whole report level.

People believed visual sensory memory could hold only four or five items, because that is how many letters people managed in whole report. They took the report score as the size of the store, and that was wrong. Sperling (1960) showed with partial report that nearly every row was available at first, so the whole scene was registered. The limit was in how much could be reported before the image faded, not in how much was stored.

An icon is the visual form of sensory memory, a fleeting mental image of what you just saw. An echo is the auditory form, the brief continuation of a sound in the auditory system after you hear it. They work the same way, each holding raw input for less than a second so there is time to process it. The difference is just the sense involved: icon for seeing, echo for hearing.

They had participants count backward by threes to block maintenance rehearsal. Participants saw three letters and a number, then counted backward from the number during a delay of 3 to 18 seconds before recalling the letters. Counting takes steady attention and keeps the inner voice busy, so the letters cannot be repeated or refreshed. Without it, people would just repeat the trigram and recall it perfectly, and the delay would tell you nothing about duration.

On the first trial, recall stayed very high even after 18 seconds, only slightly below recall after 3 seconds. Many trials later, recall after 18 seconds had dropped to close to zero, while recall after 3 seconds was still high. The delay and the counting task were exactly the same each time. The difference is that many earlier trigrams had piled up in memory and were competing with the new one.

That is proactive interference. Older information, the earlier trigrams, disrupts memory for the newer information, the current letters. The trigrams are all similar, so they are easy to confuse, and each new trial adds one more competitor. The longer the delay, the more the older trigrams win out. Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959) were looking for decay, but this build-up across trials showed interference too.

The difference is the direction of the disruption. In retroactive interference, a new memory interferes with remembering old information, like a new phone number crowding out your old one. In proactive interference, an old memory interferes with remembering new information, like last week's parking spots making it harder to find where you parked today. Retro means backward and pro means forward. In both cases the more similar the memories, the stronger the competition.

The average over all trials makes it look like a steady loss with time, as though short-term memory simply decays. But the average mixes very different trials together. Early trials have high recall even at 18 seconds, and later trials have very low recall at 18 seconds. The steep drop comes mostly from the later trials, where proactive interference is strongest, so averaging hides interference behind something that looks like decay.

Miller (1956) proposed that short-term memory can hold seven, plus or minus two, units. The key word is units, not raw items. A unit can be a digit, a word, a multi-digit number, or even a phrase, and each one counts as a single slot. The plus or minus two allows for differences between people and kinds of material. That became the classic estimate of short-term memory capacity.

Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) found that capacity depends on how complex the objects are. Visual memory held about 4.4 colored squares, but only about 2.8 Chinese characters, about 2.0 random polygons, and about 1.6 shaded cubes. So the more complex the object, the fewer you can hold. Each object still counts as one item, but more detail uses up more of the limited capacity, which supports capacity depending on the amount of information.

Chase and Simon (1973) compared chess masters and beginners, and they also compared two kinds of boards: arrangements that could occur in a real game and random arrangements. With real positions, the master placed about three times as many pieces correctly as the beginner. With random boards, they did about the same and both recalled few. So the master's advantage comes from chunking with chess knowledge, not from a bigger short-term memory.

Ericsson and colleagues (1980) trained a college student who was a runner, and his digit span rose to 79. He did it by chunking the digits into meaningful running times. His short-term memory still held only a few units, as everyone's does, but each unit was a race time packed with several digits. Normal span is near seven, so knowledge from long-term memory is what stretched it.

A chunk is a meaningful unit that combines smaller pieces, and however many pieces it contains, it takes up a single slot. So the store itself stays the same size, but each slot carries more. What makes a group meaningful is knowledge in long-term memory, so the more someone knows, the larger the chunks they can form. That is why a skilled chess player holds familiar clusters of pieces as single chunks.

Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed working memory, which resembles short-term memory but covers much more. It is a limited-capacity system for the temporary storage and manipulation of information in complex tasks like comprehension, learning, and reasoning. The old view treated short-term memory as passive storage, a kind of waiting room. Working memory instead has parts that hold information while you work on it, with storage and manipulation sharing one limited capacity.

The central executive stores nothing itself. It directs and maintains attention, coordinates the other components, pulls in knowledge from long-term memory, and suppresses irrelevant information. It also does things like calculations. The phonological loop, by contrast, is a store for verbal and auditory information, with a phonological store and an articulatory rehearsal process that silently repeats items like an inner voice so they do not fade.

Multiplying 43 times 6 in your head means holding information while also working on it. You multiply 3 by 6 to get 18, hold the 8 in memory, and carry the 1 to the 4. Then you multiply 6 by 4 to get 24, add the carried 1 to get 25, and combine that with the held 8 to make 258. Holding the 8 is storage, and carrying and calculating are processing.

Baddeley added the episodic buffer in 2000. It is a fourth component with a limited capacity of about four chunks, and it binds information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into integrated episodes. It was needed because people can recall about 16 words of a meaningful sentence, and because some amnesic patients can recall a story they just heard. The original model had nowhere to keep those.

In Atkinson and Shiffrin's model, short-term memory is a single component for all types of information, used mainly for holding things briefly. Working memory is built from several cooperating parts: a central executive, a phonological loop, and a visuospatial sketchpad, with the episodic buffer added later. It is for manipulating information during reasoning, comprehension, and learning. With separate stores, a verbal task and a visual task can run together with little interference.

Conrad (1964) found that when people saw letters briefly and wrote them down, their errors followed sound, not appearance. They were unlikely to replace a letter with one that looked like it, such as writing F for E, and likely to replace it with one that sounded like it, such as writing B for E. The letters came in through the eyes, but they were held as sound codes in the phonological loop.

Conrad (1964) manipulated whether the flashed letters were similar or not similar, with half of the presentations each. Participants saw target letters quickly flashed and then wrote them down. The letters vanished so fast that writing them depended on memory. Lists of similar-sounding letters led to more errors than lists of distinct-sounding letters, and the errors that did happen were sound-alike substitutions.

The word-length effect is that memory for lists is better for short words than for long words. Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984) found it. Long words take more time to say, so fewer of them can be rehearsed before they fade. The idea is that the loop holds roughly what you can say in about 1.5 to 2 seconds, so the limit is one of time rather than a fixed number of items.

Ellis and Hennelly (1980) found that the children had a shorter digit span in Welsh than in English. The children knew the same numbers in both languages, so the difference was not about knowledge. Welsh number names simply take longer to pronounce, and so fewer of them can be rehearsed in the roughly 1.5 to 2 seconds the phonological loop can hold. The limit is speaking time, not the numbers themselves.

Articulatory suppression, speaking while you memorize, keeps the phonological loop busy, and it makes memory worse. It also reduces both the word-length effect and the phonological similarity effect. The word-length effect shrinks because rehearsal is blocked, so short words lose their advantage. The similarity effect shrinks because seen letters are no longer converted into sound codes. One manipulation removes both, which suggests rehearsal and recoding share the same speech-based system.

answers.topic: Spatial representations and Brooks’s response reversal
answers: Brooks (1968) found a reversal. In the sentence task, people held a sentence and judged each word as a noun or not, and pointing was easier than speaking. In the F task, people held the image of a block F and judged whether each corner was an inside or outside corner, and speaking was easier than pointing. So neither response was easier overall. What mattered was whether the response used the same kind of memory as the task.

Brooks (1968) manipulated the response mode, speaking versus pointing, across two memory tasks. In the sentence task, participants memorized a sentence and indicated yes or no for whether each word was a noun. In the F task, they memorized a block letter F and moved around its corners, indicating inside or outside corners. The task stayed the same within each experiment, and only the way of responding changed.

With the sentence, the phonological loop was already busy holding and working through the words, and speaking also needs the loop, so the two competed. Pointing relies on the sketchpad, which was free. With the F, it was the other way around. The image sat in the sketchpad, and pointing means looking and moving the hand to places on a sheet, which uses those same spatial resources, while speaking used the free loop.

It suggests that verbal and visuospatial memory are somewhat independent, with at least separate capacities. Tasks were easier when the memory and the response used different systems, and harder when they used the same one. Filling the phonological loop leaves the sketchpad room to spare, and the reverse. Each part interferes with itself far more than with the other, which a single store could not produce.

Holding the shape of an F uses the visuospatial sketchpad, which holds visual and spatial information such as shape, appearance, and layout. That is why, in Brooks's (1968) F task, pointing was harder, since it needed the same spatial resources, and speaking was easier, because the phonological loop was free to help.

Shepard and Metzler (1971) found that reaction time grew steadily with the angle of rotation between two objects. Pairs at 0 degrees took about 1 second, and pairs at 180 degrees took about 4.5 seconds, with reaction time rising in a straight line in between. Participants mentally rotated one object to line it up with the other, so a bigger difference in angle needed a longer rotation, as though the image turned at a steady speed.

Picture-plane rotation turns the object flat within the page, much like the hand of a clock. Depth rotation turns the object as if it were spun around a vertical axis, which is a rotation in three-dimensional space. Shepard and Metzler (1971) found the same straight-line increase in reaction time with angle for both, so the mental image is handled as a three-dimensional object, with the work done in the visuospatial sketchpad.

These are the three functions the central executive is often split into, following Miyake and colleagues (2000). Updating replaces old contents of working memory with new, relevant information. Shifting means moving between tasks or mental sets. Inhibition means holding back unwanted thoughts or responses. Splitting the executive this way gives specific functions that can be measured separately and that vary between people.

A homunculus is a little person in the head who makes every decision. Saying that a central executive directs attention and controls everything names the control without explaining how it works, so it can look like an empty explanation. Breaking the executive into updating, shifting, and inhibition answers that criticism, because those are specific functions that can be measured separately.

That is inhibition, one of the central executive's functions from Miyake and colleagues (2000). It means holding back unwanted thoughts or responses, so distractions do not use up working memory. The executive suppresses irrelevant information so the limited space stays available for what the current task needs, which keeps attention on the goal.

answers.topic: Integrated episodes and filtering individual differences
answers: The episodic buffer is a fourth component of working memory, added by Baddeley in 2000. It binds information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory into integrated episodes, joining separate pieces into one combined memory. Its capacity is limited, about four chunks, where a chunk is a meaningful unit that may contain several pieces. It sits between the loop and the sketchpad so their contents can be combined.

Vogel and colleagues (2005) found that high-capacity people showed greater brain activity for four relevant items than for two, and adding irrelevant blue bars had no effect, so they kept distractors out. Low-capacity people were different. When distractors were added, their activity rose to nearly the level for four targets, so they let the distractors in, where they took up space meant for the targets.

Vogel and colleagues (2005) first sorted participants into high-capacity and low-capacity groups, then manipulated the display. There were three conditions: two relevant red bars, four relevant red bars, and two red bars with two irrelevant blue bars to ignore. They measured an ERP, electrical brain activity from the scalp, during the blank delay, which tracks how much a person is holding. People judged whether a red bar's angle had changed.

They are positively related. Filtering efficiency is an EEG measure of how well someone keeps irrelevant items out of working memory, and it correlates with capacity, so people with higher capacity are less distracted by irrelevant items. The people who hold more are the same people who screen out what they do not need. So effective capacity reflects both the size of the store and the strength of the filter.

Amnesia is a severe loss of long-term memory, so these patients cannot store the story in long-term memory. Yet they can recall a story they just heard, which means it was held in working memory as a meaningful episode. That needs a component large enough to contain it, and that is the episodic buffer, which binds information into integrated episodes. The original model had nowhere to keep it.

A problem is an obstacle between a present state and a goal, where the solution is not immediately obvious. The present state is the way things are now, the goal is the way we want them to be, and the obstacle is whatever stops us from going straight there. In the sliding-tile puzzle, for example, the scrambled board is the present state, the ordered board is the goal, and the rule that a tile can only move into the empty space is the obstacle.

Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) found different patterns. For algebra problems, warmth rose gradually, climbing steadily over the last minute until the solution, so those were solved step by step. For insight problems, warmth stayed low until just before the answer and then jumped sharply, from about 3 to 7. People felt cold only seconds before solving them, so their sense of closeness was a poor guide.

Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) manipulated the type of problem. Insight problems, the triangle problem and the chain problem, were compared with noninsight problems, which were algebra problems. Participants gave warmth judgments every 15 seconds, rating from cold to hot how close they felt to the answer. The warmth ratings track the feeling of closeness over time, which shows whether the answer came gradually or suddenly.

Restructuring is reorganizing the problem's representation so it is seen in a new way. The elements stay the same, but the way the solver arranges them changes. In Köhler's circle problem, you are asked for the length of line x when the radius is r. Seen as a lone line, x is hard. Seen as a diagonal of a rectangle, whose other diagonal is a radius, x equals r, because a rectangle's two diagonals are equal.

In both problems the obvious approach fails and the answer comes only when the parts are seen differently. In the chain problem, opening one link on each of four pieces costs 20 cents, over the 15 cent budget. You have to treat one whole piece as a set of connectors, opening all three of its links to join the other three pieces. In the triangle problem, you have to see how three dots can be moved so the same triangle points down.

answers.topic: Fixation, functional fixedness, and mental set
answers: The empty matchbox condition removed the cue that made the box look like a container. In the candle problem, full matchboxes looked only like containers for matches, and that familiar function kept people from using them as supports. When participants were given empty matchboxes, they were twice as likely to solve the problem. An empty box no longer looks like a container in use, so its flat bottom is easier to notice as a shelf for the candle.

Functional fixedness is restricting the use of an object to its familiar functions, so you see one purpose and overlook other possible uses. In the two-string problem, people think of pliers as a gripping tool, and that hides the fact that they are heavy. The solution needs that weight, tying the pliers to one string to make a pendulum and catching it as it swings. The pliers are in plain view the whole time.

A mental set is a preconceived notion about how to approach a problem, based on past experience with that problem or similar ones. In the water-jug problems, the formula B minus A minus twice C solved each early problem, so people kept using it automatically. Later, in problem 7 the answer 18 is simply A plus C, and in problem 8 the answer 25 is simply A minus C, but the set inhibited people from seeing those simpler solutions.

That is a mental set. A method that worked before gets used again, even when a simpler one is available. In the water-jug problems, repeated success with B minus A minus twice C builds a habit, and the familiar method still works on the later problems, so nothing signals that anything is wrong. But it hides the easier route. Past success becomes an obstacle in its own right.

Both are kinds of obstacles to solving, but they differ in what is stuck. Functional fixedness is about an object, restricting it to its familiar use, like seeing the matchbox only as a container or the pliers only as a gripper. A mental set is about a method, a way of solving that worked before and gets used again, like repeating B minus A minus twice C. Fixation is the broader tendency, and fixedness and set are two forms of it.

answers.topic: Problem spaces, operators, and means–end analysis
answers: Newell and Simon describe every problem space as having three kinds of states. The initial state holds the conditions at the beginning of the problem. Intermediate states are the conditions partway through, after some moves but before the answer. The goal state is the solution. To solve a problem is to travel through this space, starting at the initial state and making moves that reach intermediate states, until the search arrives at the goal state.

Operators are the rules that specify which moves are allowed and which are not, and they take the problem from one state to another. In the Tower of Hanoi there are three rules: disks are moved one at a time from one peg to another, a disk can be moved only when nothing is on top of it, and a larger disk cannot go on a smaller one. Every legal move applies one of these operators.

A subgoal is a smaller goal that must be met before the main goal can be reached, and it creates an intermediate state closer to the goal. In the Tower of Hanoi, the first subgoal is to free the large disk, the second is to free the third peg, and the third is to move the large disk onto the third peg. Each subgoal removes one obstacle to moving the largest disk.

Means-end analysis tries to reduce the difference between the current state and the goal state. At each point the solver asks how the current state differs from the goal and which move would shrink that difference. When no move can close the main difference directly, the solver sets a subgoal that removes the obstacle. This steers the search toward the goal, so the solver does not have to try every possible move.

A search tree lays out the problem space of the tile puzzle. Each state is a point in the tree, and each legal move links one state to the next. The starting board allows three moves, so the tree splits three ways, and then keeps branching at every level. It shows how quickly the possibilities multiply while only one path leads to the goal, which is why a good strategy follows the branches that bring the board closer to the goal.

The key is color. Each domino covers two neighboring squares, which are always different colors, so every domino covers one dark square and one light one. Opposite corners share the same color, so removing them leaves 32 squares of one color and 30 of the other. Thirty-one dominoes would need 31 squares of each color. The numbers seem to fit, since 62 squares match 31 dominoes, but the colors do not.

The conditions differed in what information was on the squares: a blank board, a colored board, a board labeled black and pink, and a board labeled bread and butter. The board and dominoes were identical in all four. Participants solved the bread and butter condition twice as fast as the blank condition. So wording that pointed toward the right representation made the problem easier, even though nothing about the problem itself had changed.

The labels bread and butter emphasized the difference between the two kinds of squares, since bread and butter naturally come in pairs, one of each. That helped solvers see each domino as pairing one square of each kind, which is the constraint that makes the covering impossible. A small change in wording guided people toward the representation that solves the problem, and they solved it twice as fast as with a blank board.

A think-aloud protocol is a method where participants say aloud what they are thinking while they solve a problem, putting new thoughts into words as they come. It reveals what information the person is attending to, so researchers can follow what the solver notices and when. With the checkerboard, solvers first talked about laying down dominoes, then about pairing the two kinds of squares. That shows restructuring while it happens.

That is restructuring, the Gestalt idea of a change in representation. In the mutilated checkerboard, the board and the rules do not change, but the solver stops thinking about laying down dominoes and starts thinking about pairing the two kinds of squares. Once each domino is seen as covering one square of each kind, the unequal counts of the two colors become available, and the answer follows from a simple count.
